segments.narration: In 1968, the research submersible Alvin sank into the Atlantic Ocean after its support ship's cables snapped during transport.
While diving 2,000 feet beneath the surface, the vessel shuddered as a massive creature slammed into it.
Crew members scrambled, staring at instruments as something violently rammed the titanium hull.
When the craft returned to the surface, they found an astonishing calling card: a broadbill swordfish had driven its sharp bill into the sub's skin and wedged itself firmly there.
The terrifying attack wasn't a monster of the deep, but an aggressive swordfish that mistook the sub's metallic hum for a rival and jammed itself right into the hull.

accuracy_flags.claim: In 1966, the research submersible Alvin vanished mid-dive.
accuracy_flags.note: Alvin did not vanish in 1966. It was lost during transport on October 26, 1968, when the support ship Lulu's cables snapped while lowering it, causing it to sink.

accuracy_flags.claim: The sub was dangling from steel cables when violent jaws bit into it.
accuracy_flags.note: The swordfish attack happened on July 6, 1967, at 2,000 feet below the surface during dive 202—not while dangling from support cables just beneath the surface.

accuracy_flags.claim: Marine biologists discovered massive swordfish bills embedded in deep-sea cables.
accuracy_flags.note: The swordfish attacked the submersible itself and became trapped in its skin/rigging, not in deep-sea cables.

accuracy_flags.claim: A swordfish had thrust its bill directly through the titanium hull and steel framework.
accuracy_flags.note: The source states the swordfish became trapped in Alvin's 'skin' (not its titanium sphere pressure hull, which is 2 inches thick and impenetrable to a swordfish bill).
